repreve.origin: REPREVE is a brand of Unifi, Inc., a yarn producer based in Greensboro, North Carolina, launched in 2007. Most REPREVE products are recycled polyester, poly(ethylene terephthalate), made largely from post-consumer PET bottles; the platform also includes recycled nylon and products made from textile and yarn waste. Unifi's plant at Yadkinville, North Carolina, converts bottles into REPREVE yarn, and a Reidsville facility handles bottle recycling, according to trade reporting.
repreve.structure: Recycled PET is chemically the same polyester as virgin PET: a condensation polymer of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid linked by ester bonds, with rigid aromatic rings that give stiffness, a glass transition well above room temperature and a crystalline melting range far above normal laundering temperatures. Mechanical recycling can shorten chains (lower intrinsic viscosity), which spinners compensate for by solid-state polymerization or blending. Filament cross-sections may be round or engineered; REPREVE fiber also carries Unifi's proprietary FiberPrint tracer additive.
repreve.process: The bottle route is mechanical recycling: bottles are collected, sorted, labels and caps removed, and the PET is ground to flake, washed and dried. Flake is melted, filtered and extruded as chip or directly as filament, which is drawn and textured into yarn or cut into staple. A tracer, FiberPrint, is added during extrusion so that REPREVE content can later be detected, and Unifi's U-TRUST program tests finished goods for it. Unifi has also described work on fiber-to-fiber recycling of textile waste.
repreve.performance: Performance matches conventional polyester: high strength that is nearly unchanged when wet, low moisture regain (well under 1%), quick drying, good dimensional stability after heat-setting, and resistance to many chemicals. It is thermoplastic and melts rather than chars. Dyeing requires disperse dyes at high temperature or with carriers because the dense, hydrophobic polymer lacks ionic sites. Pilling can be an issue in staple fabrics because strong fibers do not break away. Environmental comparisons published by Unifi are producer claims.
repreve.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: polyester melts and shrinks from flame, burns with sooty smoke and a sweetish odor, leaving a hard bead. FTIR identifies PET. Recycled PET cannot be reliably told from virgin PET by routine methods; REPREVE content is instead verified by detecting Unifi's FiberPrint tracer through the U-TRUST program. Confusion arises when 'made with REPREVE' is read as meaning the whole garment is recycled.
repreve.labeling: REPREVE is a trademark, not a generic name. US labels must state polyester (or nylon) under the TFPIA and 16 CFR Part 303, and EU labels must use polyester or polyamide under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Recycled-content statements must be substantiated and should state the share. Unifi's U-TRUST verification is a producer program; any independent recycled-content certification should be confirmed for the specific product.
repreve.past: Unifi, a long-established North Carolina textured-yarn maker, launched REPREVE in 2007, using yarn waste and bottle-grade PET as feedstock. The brand grew into a prominent recycled-fiber ingredient name in apparel, supported by its own bottle processing in Yadkinville and by the FiberPrint tracer and U-TRUST verification. Its history mirrors the rise of bottle-to-fiber recycling, which diverts PET from landfill but does not close a textile loop; Unifi has since described efforts toward textile-to-textile recycling.
facts: post-consumer PET bottles, plus yarn and textile waste

seaqual.origin: SEAQUAL is the brand of the SEAQUAL INITIATIVE, a Spanish-origin program set up in 2016 by the Ecoalf foundation, the textile group Santanderina and the spinning company Antex. The underlying generic fiber is recycled polyester (PET). According to the initiative, SEAQUAL YARN is 100% post-consumer recycled polyester, of which roughly 10% is SEAQUAL MARINE PLASTIC recovered from marine litter and roughly 90% comes from other post-consumer PET such as bottles. The initiative names ANTEX (Spain) and VICA (Mexico) as its yarn manufacturing partners.
seaqual.structure: The polymer is poly(ethylene terephthalate), a polyester of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid joined by ester bonds, identical in chemistry to other recycled or virgin PET. Marine-recovered plastic is mixed plastics when collected; only the PET fraction suitable for melt processing ends up in the polymer. Degradation from sun and seawater can lower molecular weight, which is one reason the marine share is a minority blended with land-sourced post-consumer PET. The initiative states that its yarn contains a tracer to link material to collection projects.
seaqual.process: As the initiative describes it, fishing crews and clean-up projects bring marine litter ashore, where it is sorted; PET is separated, cleaned and processed into flake and then into SEAQUAL MARINE PLASTIC, which is blended with other post-consumer PET. The blended polymer is melt-extruded into filament or staple fiber and spun into yarn by licensed partners, then sold to fabric makers and brands that join the initiative. The Ecoalf foundation's Upcycling the Oceans project was an early source of marine litter for the program.
seaqual.performance: Fabrics behave like any polyester of comparable yarn and construction: strength that is retained when wet, very low moisture regain, fast drying, dimensional stability after heat-setting, and dyeing with disperse dyes at high temperature. It melts rather than chars. The small marine-plastic share does not give different performance. The initiative's life-cycle comparisons (reported reductions in CO2, water and electricity against virgin polyester) are producer claims based on its own assessment boundaries.
seaqual.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: PET melts, drips, burns with sooty smoke and leaves a hard bead. FTIR identifies polyester, but no routine test separates marine-derived PET from other recycled or virgin PET. Verification relies on the initiative's tracer, its partner licensing and documentation. Mislabeling risk lies in describing a SEAQUAL fabric as made from ocean plastic when the marine fraction is a minority of the yarn and the fabric may contain other fibers.
seaqual.labeling: SEAQUAL is a program trademark, not a generic fiber name. US labels must state polyester under the TFPIA and 16 CFR Part 303, and EU labels polyester under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Claims such as 'made with marine plastic' must be truthful and substantiated with the actual marine and recycled shares for the specific product. Any recycled-content certification should be confirmed on the certificate for the yarn or fabric in question.
seaqual.past: The SEAQUAL INITIATIVE grew out of Spanish efforts, led by the Ecoalf foundation's Upcycling the Oceans project, to have fishing boats land the plastic waste caught in their nets rather than return it to the sea. In 2016 the foundation, Santanderina and Antex established SEAQUAL to turn that litter into fiber, announcing early sales of fiber made partly from seabed waste. The program later expanded into a membership community of yarn makers, fabric mills and brands, and added SEAQUAL MARINE PLASTIC as a separate traceable input.
facts: 100% post-consumer recycled PET, about 10% of it marine plastic
